name: Marco Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, governments or political parties. We don’t sell anything or campaign, and your answers are confidential. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I supervise four project-reporting assistants inside a large energy group, and I'm new enough to the management job that my boss still sends back the priorities I set. I'm 58, have a bachelor's degree in physics and came from individual technical work; I use approved AI every day, but a tidy report hasn't taught me how to tell somebody their work isn't ready. The group pays well, my wife teaches part-time, our children are grown, and we've paid off the mortgage and built 134,400 in accessible savings against monthly costs of 4,800. There are many employers nearby, and we'd been aiming for me to finish at 65, though my own pension access and net income haven't been established.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the daily assistant can be useful without making the whole department disappear. If it helps someone spot the wrong month in a cost report, I'm not going to throw it out because the bigger story disappointed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd feel secure about our living and my job in this picture, even while I'm still learning to manage. My 6,500 take-home and my wife's 1,800 cover the 4,800 budget, including annual bills, leaving 3,500, and there's no current warning about my post. The 134,400 cash is twenty-eight months of total costs, not an assumed pension. I'd be a little disappointed that the tool didn't get much better, which is quite a comfortable thing to be disappointed about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the daily approved report assistant and the weekly review where my boss checks my work priorities. We'd continue putting the existing 3,500 monthly surplus into savings through the first year while both wages lasted. I'd keep experiments with new tools to invented data on my own device outside work, using free versions rather than buying subscriptions or moving company files.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with enough curiosity left to play with a new feature after dinner. Getting an ordinary working week right would still be satisfying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why keep the review if the assistant can write the report?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because writing the report isn't deciding which assistant has too much work or which project needs attention first. My boss still catches those mistakes, and I wouldn't replace that check with a fluent paragraph.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do the free experiments change your work process?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not automatically; they're something I enjoy at home. I'd need the employer's permission before introducing another tool or company records, rather than call a personal experiment an approved system.

say: I'd keep a **useful assistant** even if the bigger story disappointed.
I'd value finding a **wrong reporting month** rather than expect the department to disappear.
think: I consider our **living and my job** secure, despite still learning management and with no current post warning.
Our **cash reserve** isn't a pension, but financial comfort lets me feel disappointed rather than threatened by limited tool progress.
do: Keep the **approved report assistant** and existing weekly priority review during the first year.
Continue the existing **3,500 monthly saving** while both wages last.
Experiment only with **invented data** on my own device outside work using free tools, seeking permission before any workplace introduction.
feel: **Calm and curious**, satisfied by improving an ordinary working week.
S0.quote: Getting an ordinary working week right would still be satisfying.
fieldNote: He separates **tool fluency** from allocating work and retains a supervisor's check on his junior management decisions.
His **personal experiments** use no company data or paid subscriptions and confer no permission to change employer systems.

steps.text: Continue the approved assistant, priority review and existing 3,500 monthly savings transfer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say checking and writing the project reports are exactly where the change will land. I'd want us to measure corrections as well as faster drafts, and include the manager's work in that count.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could lose this post because allocating and checking reports are also thinking work, and I'm not especially strong at the allocating part. My technical past might help me compete locally while jobs still exist, but another desk isn't permanently protected. The reserve stops this being a scramble for next week's money; it doesn't make my wage safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for permission to test the approved assistant's batch-check function on six cleared old reports during two existing paid reporting sessions, without adding hours or removing my boss's sign-off. I'd run it only after my boss approved the records and scope, compare every flagged item with the originals, and report failures as well as successes. In the first year I'd also apply for actual technical reporting vacancies locally, using personal time and no company files. I'd resign only for signed terms leaving at least 5,000 take-home after extra travel, unless my wife and I separately agreed a funded lower-income plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about my place, but curious enough to want the comparison done properly. I'd rather know the tool can do my checking than find out when somebody else presents the result.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Are you already authorised to run the batch check?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I can use the ordinary assistant daily but that test needs approval of the old reports and the scope first. I'd keep the current checks if my boss said no; a request isn't a pilot that's already happened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would you consider 5,000 rather than your present 6,500?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With my wife's current 1,800 it would still exceed today's 4,800 costs, but I'd check the actual household budget before signing. I wouldn't count her teaching income if the job or hours had changed by then.

say: I'd measure **corrections and speed** when reporting tasks move to software.
I'd include the **manager's checking** rather than count only the assistants' work.
think: My **post could go** because allocating and checking reports are thinking tasks and allocation remains a weakness.
Local competition remains possible, but our **reserve** protects decision time rather than the wage itself.
do: Request a **six-report test** within two existing paid sessions; run only with approved scope/records, retaining sign-off and checking flags against originals.
Apply for actual **technical reporting vacancies** in personal time without company files.
Resign only for **signed terms** netting ≥5,000 after extra travel and a checked budget, unless we separately agree a funded lower-income plan.
feel: **Anxious and curious**, preferring an honest comparison to an unexpected staffing presentation.
S1.quote: The reserve stops this being a scramble for next week's money; it doesn't make my wage safe.
fieldNote: His **test request** uses existing paid sessions but requires separate scope and record permission before running, with supervisor sign-off retained.
His **job threshold** permits lower pay but still requires signed terms and a checked household budget using only income actually available.

steps.text: Request permission for a six-report batch-check test during two existing paid sessions
Apply to actual local technical reporting vacancies using personal time
Resign only with signed terms netting ≥5,000 after travel or a separately agreed funded household alternative

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the family that being interested in AGI doesn't mean my employer will keep paying me to watch it arrive. The reporting desk is exposed in 2028; the 2031 robot date is about a different part of the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be sixty and expect my wage to go, though our cash means I wouldn't have to accept the first bad offer. My wife's teaching also includes thinking work that AGI could change, so I can't quietly assume her 1,800 lasts. We've got twenty-eight months of today's full household costs, which is substantial time but not a life after sixty. I'd be anxious about spending the time well rather than frightened of tomorrow's food bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cancel the plan to buy a 12,000 replacement car this winter before signing any order, keeping that money inside the existing reserve. If my job ended in the first year after AGI, I'd give myself a twelve-month decision period with quarterly reviews and a maximum cash draw of 57,600, which is twelve months of today's full budget without either wage. I'd draw only actual household shortfalls, recalculate immediately if costs changed, and look at real paid vacancies before each review without assuming an offer. I wouldn't resign early, claim a pension or promise a permanent retirement just because we'd funded one year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I could make a deliberate pause instead of buying a course in a frightened afternoon. A year paid from savings is a year to decide, not proof that I've retired.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if you reach the cash cap before the year ends?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop treating the old plan as valid and redo spending and the job search with my wife immediately. The cap is a limit for review, not permission to borrow the next year's living costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would another reporting vacancy reassure you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A written offer with real work and pay could help for a time. It wouldn't make those thinking tasks immune, so I'd price the actual work rather than imagine I'd found the last safe desk.

say: I'd distinguish **interest in AGI** from being paid to watch it arrive.
I'd explain that **reporting work** is exposed before the later robot date.
think: At **sixty**, I expect wage loss but have cash to avoid the first bad offer.
My wife's **teaching income** is also exposed, and twenty-eight months of current full costs isn't a lifelong income.
do: Cancel the uncontracted **12,000 car purchase**, retaining the money inside the reserve.
After job loss, cap a **twelve-month decision period** at 57,600 in actual cash shortfalls, with quarterly reviews excluding assumed wages.
Recalculate immediately after **cost changes** or cap exhaustion, review actual vacancies, and avoid early resignation or unfunded permanent retirement.
feel: **Anxious but deliberate**, able to pause without an immediate food-bill crisis.
S2.quote: A year paid from savings is a year to decide, not proof that I've retired.
fieldNote: The **57,600 limit** budgets full costs without either wage and draws only actual shortfalls rather than assuming the teaching salary continues.
His **decision period** includes quarterly and trigger-based reviews, with neither a purchased car nor permanent retirement treated as completed.

steps.text: Fund at most twelve decision months with 57,600 maximum draws and quarterly/triggered reviews

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years makes it worth testing whether I can finish two years earlier, rather than invent a title that survives AGI. I'd rather put the pension questions on paper while someone is still paying me to work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 63 in 2031, two years before our existing target of 65, and I'd expect the reporting job to go then. Our cash and five potential earning years might make an earlier finish possible, but they don't establish pension access or income after the cash runs down. I'd be less worried about finding another title than about making the household plan honest, including my wife's own exposure before the 2034 robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move the planning target from 65 to 63 and request written pension access dates, net amounts and early-draw penalties now. I'd pay a fixed-fee independent adviser at most 900 from one month's new 3,500 surplus, leaving the 134,400 reserve untouched, to cost the gap to any confirmed pension date without assuming either future wage. I wouldn't give notice until available cash covered that whole gap plus twenty-four months of our then-current essential costs, and confirmed income afterward covered the ongoing budget and unexpected bills. In the first year after AGI I'd use that funded plan only if all the tests had been met; otherwise I'd keep seeking paid work and revise the target, not call an estimate a pension award.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but more interested in a possible finish than in hanging onto a new business card. Two fewer working years would be attractive only if we weren't borrowing them from later life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Are you counting five more years of saving as already in the bank?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the plan would use actual balances when we got there, not the result of multiplying today's surplus. Either wage could change before 2031, so I'd update the figures each year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does hiring the adviser make the retirement approved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'm buying a calculation, not an entitlement or a guaranteed investment return. The scheme has to confirm what is payable, and my wife and I have to agree the household budget before I give any notice.

say: I'd test **finishing two years earlier** rather than invent a supposedly protected title.
I'd ask the **pension questions** while wages still give us preparation time.
think: At **63**, I expect the job to go before our existing age-65 target.
Cash and potential earnings make an earlier finish conceivable, but **pension access** and income after drawdown remain unconfirmed.
do: Move the **target** from 65 to 63 and request written pension access, net amounts and early-draw penalties.
Buy fixed-fee advice up to **900 from new surplus**, protecting 134,400 and costing the gap without assumed future wages.
Give notice only with **gap plus 24-month essentials** funded, confirmed later income covering costs and surprises, and household agreement; otherwise revise.
feel: **Anxious but interested**, testing an earlier finish without borrowing from later life.
S3.quote: Two fewer working years would be attractive only if we weren't borrowing them from later life.
fieldNote: His **earlier target** advances an explicit existing plan by two years, while notice requires both bridge funding and confirmed affordable income afterward.
The **commercial advice** fee comes from new surplus, conveys no pension entitlement and is not recorded as government or community support.

steps.text: Advance the retirement planning target from 65 to 63
Give notice only with cash-funded pension gap, 24-month essentials, confirmed affordable later income and household agreement
Seek paid work if actual bridge funding or confirmed ongoing pension income fails the budget test

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the extra decade may let people our age finish before AGI, but only if they've checked the money rather than the calendar. I'd rather discuss a workable handover than claim the last three years of a job nobody has promised me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 68 in 2036, three years beyond our existing target of 65, which makes the timetable much easier to imagine. I still don't know the pension terms, so I can't say now that work and living would be secure then. My wife's teaching work could change before the 2039 robots too; a longer date doesn't turn either wage into permanent income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd request written retirement figures for our existing target of 65 now and review actual income, costs and cash annually with my wife, without assuming ten years of salaries. I'd keep working and saving the existing surplus while both wages lasted, and give notice only after any gap to confirmed income was funded and the ongoing budget, including unexpected bills, was covered. I'd also set a ceiling of 1,800 a year from new surplus for a family gathering, with dates agreed by our grown children and no non-refundable booking before leave approval or an agreed funded retirement date. In the first year after AGI we'd recheck actual income before repeating that spending and seek paid work if retirement funding hadn't materialised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the unconfirmed income, but less absorbed by the employer's next announcement. I'd like the family gathering to be something we can afford, not a celebration charged to the years after it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you count the family gathering as an investment in retirement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, it's spending on time together, and the children may not be free on the dates we suggest. If the income changed we'd reduce or cancel an uncommitted plan rather than call affection a reason to ignore the budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Are you changing your existing stopping age here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not in this picture; the existing 65 target already comes before AGI at 68. It still needs confirmed income and gap funding, but I don't need to bring the date forward simply to get ahead of 2036.

say: I'd distinguish a **checked retirement budget** from a calendar that merely looks favourable.
I'd discuss a **workable handover** without assuming the employer promises every remaining year.
think: At **68**, AGI follows our existing age-65 target, but unconfirmed pension terms prevent me calling future living secure.
My wife's **teaching wage** can change before later robots, so neither salary becomes permanent because the date is distant.
do: Review written **age-65 pension terms**, actual cash and costs annually; give notice only with funded gaps and confirmed affordable ongoing income.
Continue existing **saving while paid**, without assuming ten more earning years.
Cap **family gatherings** at 1,800 yearly from new surplus, requiring family dates and leave/funded-retirement agreement before non-refundable bookings; reassess after income changes.
feel: **Anxious but less absorbed**, making room for affordable family time.
S4.quote: I'd like the family gathering to be something we can afford, not a celebration charged to the years after it.
fieldNote: He keeps the existing **65 target**, so this scenario doesn't invent an earlier-retirement action just because AGI arrives at 68.
His **family spending** uses capped new surplus, shared dates and booking permission, with reassessment after income changes rather than investment claims.

steps.text: Continue existing savings while both wages last pending confirmed retirement funding
Plan family gatherings under the 1,800 new-surplus, shared-date and booking-permission gates
Seek paid work if funded retirement has not materialised after AGI

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because at sixty I might be asked to leave before I'd decided what a useful next stage looked like. I'd want written leaving dates, the actual pension figures and permission to use my notice period for interviews if I needed them; that permission isn't agreed today. I have room to make a decision, and I don't want to confuse that with having made one.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether someone who enjoys the technology is also any good at the job around it. My assistants don't need another clever summary when I've given all four of them the same deadline. I'd like to be judged on whether the work gets organised, not whether I found the newest menu.

headlineQuote: My assistants don't need another clever summary when I've given all four of them the same deadline.
portrait: Marco is **58**, a junior reporting manager with a physics bachelor's degree, still weak at priorities and difficult staff conversations.
He uses **AI daily** and receives high pay on his employer's scale, without claiming expertise in managing four assistants.
He and his **part-time teacher wife** have grown children, a paid-off home and twenty-eight months of current expenses accessible.
He prefers **costed choices** to either technological slogans or automatic retirement, with a limited pause and a possible earlier funded exit.
biggestWorry: I fear **AGI by 2028** most because losing work at sixty might precede deciding what comes next.
whatWouldHelp: I need **written dates**, actual pension figures and agreed interview access during notice if required.
